RAZI:1:7/r13.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r13.speaker: ابن جني
RAZI:1:7/r13.claim: Ibn Jinnī derives lugha from laghawtu, meaning I spoke, and proposes an original form ending in wāw, supported by related forms such as kurra and qulla.
RAZI:1:7/r13.anchor: قال ابن جني رحمه الله تعالى : اللغة فعلة من لغوت أي : تلكمت

RAZI:1:7/r14.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r14.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r14.claim: Razi supplements Ibn Jinnī with all six permutations of ل غ و and suggests their shared sense is deep engagement or immersion in something.
RAZI:1:7/r14.anchor: ويشبه أن يكون القدر المشترك بين الكل هو الإمعان في الشيء والخوض التام فيه

RAZI:1:7/r15.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r15.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r15.claim: He treats lafẓ, literally throwing, as metaphorical for spoken sounds: breath is expelled, and the letters produced by that breath are as if thrown outward.
RAZI:1:7/r15.anchor: وأقول : أظن أن إطلاق اللفظ على هذه الأصوات والحروف على سبيل المجاز

RAZI:1:7/r16.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r16.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r16.claim: The permutations of ʿ-b-r share crossing or transition: speech moves between letters and transfers meaning to a hearer, with related examples including tears, crossing, and interpretation.
RAZI:1:7/r16.anchor: وتركيبها من «ع ب ر » وهي في تقاليبها الستة تفيد العبور والانتقال

RAZI:1:7/r17.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r17.speaker: النحويون
RAZI:1:7/r17.claim: Most grammarians define kalima as a single word and kalām as a meaningful sentence; Ibn Jinnī sides with them, though Razi finds his evidence weak.
RAZI:1:7/r17.anchor: قال أكثر النحوين : الكلمة غير الكلام ، فالكلمة هي اللفظة المفردة

RAZI:1:7/r18.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r18.speaker: الأصوليون
RAZI:1:7/r18.claim: Most legal theorists see no difference between kalima and kalām: either term may cover a single utterance or a compound expression.
RAZI:1:7/r18.anchor: وقال أكثر الأصوليين إنه لا فرق بينهما ، فكل واحد منهما يتناول المفرد والمركب

RAZI:1:7/r19.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r19.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r19.claim: Razi judges Ibn Jinnī's case for distinguishing kalima from kalām weak, resting chiefly on an implication he draws from a statement by Sībawayh.
RAZI:1:7/r19.anchor: وما رأيت في كلامه حجة قوية في الفرق

RAZI:1:7/r20.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r20.speaker: الأصوليون
RAZI:1:7/r20.claim: Legal theorists argue that a single word counts as speech because it opposes silence, affects a listener through meaning, and can naturally be described as something a person said.
RAZI:1:7/r20.anchor: العقلاء قد اتفقوا على أن الكلام ما يضاد الخرس والسكوت

RAZI:1:7/r21.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r21.speaker: زفر
RAZI:1:7/r21.claim: In an unconsummated marriage, Zufar says that repeating the conditional phrase إن كلمتك completes the condition before the divorce clause, so the ensuing divorce does not take effect.
RAZI:1:7/r21.anchor: وحجة زفر أنه لما قال في المرة الثانية إن كلمتك

RAZI:1:7/r22.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r22.speaker: أبو حنيفة
RAZI:1:7/r22.claim: Abū Ḥanīfa and his two companions treat the condition as incomplete until the whole sentence is finished, so one divorce takes effect when the sentence is complete.

RAZI:1:7/r23.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r23.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r23.claim: Razi says the disagreement applies to إن كلمتك فأنت طالق; with إن تكلمت بكلمة, إن نطقت, إن تلفظت بلفظة, or إن قلت قولا, Zufar's view should prevail unanimously.
RAZI:1:7/r23.anchor: وجب أن يكون الحق في جميع هذه المسائل قول زفر قولا واحدا

RAZI:1:7/r24.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r24.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r24.claim: Scholars disagree whether kalima and kalām include meaningless speech: some say yes because it can be called unused or unintelligible speech, while others require meaningful expression.
RAZI:1:7/r24.anchor: لفظ الكلمة والكلام هل يتناول المهمل أم لا ؟

RAZI:1:7/r25.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r25.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r25.claim: Scholars also dispute whether naturally meaningful sounds, such as pain cries, coughs, or bird calls, count as words; the issue affects whether hearing one triggers an oath.
RAZI:1:7/r25.anchor: فهل تسمى أمثالها كلمات ؟ وكذلك صوت القطا يشبه كأنه يقول قطا

RAZI:1:7/r26.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r26.speaker: ابن جني
RAZI:1:7/r26.claim: Ibn Jinnī says qawl literally applies to a sentence or a single word, kalām only to a complete sentence, and kalima only to an isolated word; a poem treating qāf as a qawl supports the first distinction.
RAZI:1:7/r26.anchor: قال ابن جني : لفظ القول يقع على الكلام التام ، وعلى الكلمة الواحدة

RAZI:1:7/r27.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r27.speaker: ابن جني
RAZI:1:7/r27.claim: Ibn Jinnī says qawl can metaphorically mean a belief or opinion, as in attributing a doctrine to Abū Ḥanīfa or Mālik, because belief is apprehended through its expression.
RAZI:1:7/r27.anchor: لفظ القول يصح جعله مجازا عن الاعتقادات والآراء

RAZI:1:7/r28.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r28.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r28.claim: Qāla can be used for nonverbal events, as when birds, eyes, or a full basin are said to speak; Razi also cites two Qurʾānic examples of such speech.
RAZI:1:7/r28.anchor: لفظ قال قد يستعمل في غير النطق

RAZI:1:7/r29.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r29.speaker: مثبتو كلام النفس
RAZI:1:7/r29.claim: Those who affirm inner speech say the inward meaning is itself called kalām and qawl; they cite the hypocrites' false claim to be witnesses and Umar's recollection of an inwardly prepared speech.
RAZI:1:7/r29.anchor: فوجب أن يقال إنهم كانوا كاذبين في كلام آخر سوى اللفظ

RAZI:1:7/r30.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r30.speaker: عمر
RAZI:1:7/r30.claim: A report from ʿUmar says that at the Saqīfa he had composed words within himself, but Abū Bakr spoke first; Razi gives no grading.
RAZI:1:7/r30.anchor: ما نقل أن عمر قال يوم السقيفة : كنت قد زورت في نفسي كلاما

RAZI:1:7/r31.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r31.speaker: الأخطل
RAZI:1:7/r31.claim: The poet al-Akhṭal is cited for the claim that speech resides in the heart and the tongue serves as its guide; Razi gives no grading.
RAZI:1:7/r31.anchor: وأما الشاعر فقول الأخطل : إن الكلام لفي الفؤاد وإنما

RAZI:1:7/r32.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r32.speaker: من أنكر كلام النفس
RAZI:1:7/r32.claim: Those denying inner speech argue that someone who neither speaks nor pronounces letters is described as not having spoken, and that oaths attach to uttered words.
RAZI:1:7/r32.anchor: بأن من لم ينطق ولم يتلفظ بالحروف يقال إنه لم يتكلم

RAZI:1:7/r33.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r33.speaker: بعض أصحابنا
RAZI:1:7/r33.claim: Some of Razi's school hold that qawl and kalām are equivocal terms for both the inward meaning and the spoken expression.
RAZI:1:7/r33.anchor: ومن أصحابنا من قال : اسم القول والكلام مشترك بين المعنى النفساني وبين اللفظ اللساني

RAZI:1:7/r34.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r34.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r34.claim: Utterances are called aḥādīth because their successive letters occur one after another, or because hearing them brings knowledge and meanings into hearts.
RAZI:1:7/r34.anchor: هذه الكلمات والعبارات قد تسمى أحاديث

RAZI:1:7/r35.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r35.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r35.claim: Razi lists kalima, kalām, qawl, lafẓ, ʿibāra, ḥadīth, and nuṭq as terms needing comparison, leaving the derivation and precise relation of nuṭq for inquiry.
RAZI:1:7/r35.anchor: وسابعها النطق ويجب البحث عن كيفية اشتقاقه

RAZI:1:7/r36.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r36.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r36.claim: Razi rejects al-Zamakhsharī's definition of kalima as an utterance denoting one simple meaning by convention: past-tense forms and imperative particles convey more than one element.
RAZI:1:7/r36.anchor: الكلمة هي اللفظة الدالة على معنى مفرد بالوضع ، وهذا التعريف ليس بجيد

RAZI:1:7/r37.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r37.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r37.claim: Used expressions divide into a simple form, a compound whose parts signify only in another analysis, and a composed expression whose parts signify independently in every analysis.

RAZI:1:7/r38.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r38.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r38.claim: Meaningful sound has four form-meaning combinations: both simple, both compound, simple form with compound meaning, or compound form with compound meaning; compound form with simple meaning is impossible.
RAZI:1:7/r38.anchor: المسموع المفيد ينقسم إلى أربعة أقسام

RAZI:1:7/r39.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r39.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r39.claim: Razi defines kalima as a single conventional utterance signifying a meaning; the definition excludes non-words and compounds through its four restrictions.
RAZI:1:7/r39.anchor: الكلمة هي اللفظة المفردة الدالة بالاصطلاح على معنى

RAZI:1:7/r40.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r40.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r40.claim: Razi rejects Avicenna's definition of kalima as a single meaningful sound: sound is a remote genus, whereas lafẓ is the more suitable proximate genus.
RAZI:1:7/r40.anchor: الصوت جنس بعيد ، واللفظ جنس قريب ، وإيراد الجنس القريب أولى

RAZI:1:7/r41.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r41.speaker: المعتزلة
RAZI:1:7/r41.claim: The Muʿtazila require an informative word to contain at least two letters; they explain one-letter particles as shortened forms, but Razi notes that many useful particles remain counterexamples.
RAZI:1:7/r41.anchor: قالت المعتزلة : الشرط في كون الكلمة مفيدة أن تكون مركبة من حرفين فصاعدا

RAZI:1:7/r42.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r42.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r42.claim: Razi's preferred definition is anything spoken that conveys something by convention; it includes simple and compound forms while excluding writing and gesture.
RAZI:1:7/r42.anchor: كل منطوق به أفاد شيئا بالوضع فهو كلمة

RAZI:1:7/r43.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r43.speaker: عباد
RAZI:1:7/r43.claim: ʿAbbād holds that words naturally signify their meanings; Razi rejects this because natural properties do not vary across places and times, and answers that conventional assignments need not be unmotivated.
RAZI:1:7/r43.anchor: دلالة الألفاظ على مدلولاتها ليست ذاتية حقيقية ، خلافا لعباد

RAZI:1:7/r44.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r44.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r44.claim: Some words imitate their referents' sounds: qaṭā and laqlaq echo birds, while khaḍm and qaḍm distinguish eating moist and dry foods; Ibn Jinnī gives further examples.
RAZI:1:7/r44.anchor: وضعوا لفظ «الخضم » لأكل الرطب نحو البطيخ والقثاء ، ولفظ «القضم » لأكل اليابس

RAZI:1:7/r45.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r45.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r45.claim: Razi says one cannot decide whether language was divinely instituted: the regress argument for divine origin and the appeal to God's teaching Adam both admit alternatives.
RAZI:1:7/r45.anchor: لا يمكننا القطع بأن دلالة الألفاظ توقيفية

RAZI:1:7/r46.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r46.speaker: المعتزلة
RAZI:1:7/r46.claim: The Muʿtazila argue that conventional language must be created by humans, since necessary knowledge that God assigned words would entail necessary knowledge of God and undermine moral responsibility.
RAZI:1:7/r46.anchor: خلافا للمعتزلة ، واحتجوا بأن العلم بالصفة إذا كان ضروريا

RAZI:1:7/r47.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r47.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r47.claim: Razi answers that God could create necessary knowledge that a human assigner fixed a word's meaning without revealing that the assigner was God.
RAZI:1:7/r47.anchor: يخلق علما ضروريا في القلب بأن واضعا وضع هذا اللفظ لهذا المعنى

RAZI:1:7/r48.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r48.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r48.claim: Because the proofs are inconclusive, Razi allows that all languages are divinely instituted, all conventional, or partly each.
RAZI:1:7/r48.anchor: جوزنا أن تكون كل اللغات توقيفية وأن تكون كلها اصطلاحية

RAZI:1:7/r49.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r49.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r49.claim: A simple word cannot explain its own meaning from scratch without circularity, since recognizing its convention requires prior awareness of the word and meaning; learned association resolves the problem.
RAZI:1:7/r49.anchor: لو كان العلم بذلك المعنى مستفادا من ذلك اللفظ لزم الدور

RAZI:1:7/r50.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r50.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r50.claim: The circularity problem does not apply to compounds: convention supplies the simple meanings, and reason combines them to understand the compound.
RAZI:1:7/r50.anchor: أما التركيبات فعقلية ، فلا جرم عند سماع تلك المفردات يعتبر العقل تركيباتها

RAZI:1:7/r51.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r51.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r51.claim: Words signify mental conceptions rather than external objects: changing one's perception of a distant object changes the name used, and contradictory propositions do not make the world both old and originated.
RAZI:1:7/r51.anchor: الألفاظ تدل على المعاني ، لأن المعاني هي التي عناها العاني

RAZI:1:7/r52.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r52.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r52.claim: Not every essence can receive a name, because essences are unlimited and an unapprehended item cannot be individually conceived for naming.
RAZI:1:7/r52.anchor: لا يمكن أن تكون جميع الماهيات مسميات بالألفاظ

RAZI:1:7/r53.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r53.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r53.claim: Concepts most necessary to communicate, such as commands, prohibitions, generality, and specification, are likeliest to receive words because need supplies strong motivation.
RAZI:1:7/r53.anchor: كل معنى كانت الحاجة إلى التعبير عنه أهم ، كان وضع اللفظ بإزائه أولى

RAZI:1:7/r54.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r54.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r54.claim: A familiar word cannot name a hidden concept unknown to the public: motion names observable transition, not a subtle cause; likewise knowledge and power name the evident state, not its hidden ground.
RAZI:1:7/r54.anchor: وجب أن يقال : الحركة اسم لنفس هذا الانتقال

RAZI:1:7/r55.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r55.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r55.claim: Maʿnā denotes the mental conception intended by a speaker; an external thing is called a meaning only derivatively, as what the conception concerns.
RAZI:1:7/r55.anchor: المعنى اسم للصورة الذهنية لا للموجودات الخارجية

RAZI:1:7/r56.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r56.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r56.claim: Some distinctions cannot be defined verbally because language lacks a dedicated term, as with kinds of sweetness; private experiences are also indefinable to listeners who have never conceived them.
RAZI:1:7/r56.anchor: لا سبيل إلى تعريف هذه التفرقة بحسب اللفظ

RAZI:1:7/r57.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r57.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r57.claim: Language serves humans' need to communicate what is in their minds to obtain help; compared with writing, gestures, or clapping, speech is easy to produce, temporary, and combinatorially abundant.
RAZI:1:7/r57.anchor: فاحتاج إلى أن يعرف غيره ما في ضميره

RAZI:1:7/r58.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r58.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r58.claim: Human perfection is knowledge of truth and action upon good; the body, heart, and respiratory system serve that end, with breathing cooling the heart and expelled air becoming the material of sound.
RAZI:1:7/r58.anchor: كمال الإنسان في أن يعرف الحق لذاته ، والخير لأجل العمل به

RAZI:1:7/r59.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r59.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r59.claim: The Creator formed articulatory passages in the throat, tongue, teeth, and lips so breath produces distinct letters and limitless words containing wisdom beyond human grasp.
RAZI:1:7/r59.anchor: وخلق محابس ومقاطع للصوت في الحلق واللسان والأسنان والشفتين

RAZI:1:7/r60.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r60.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r60.claim: Spoken kalām is a conventional act by which a living agent reveals inner intentions and beliefs; inner speech, by contrast, is a real attribute like knowledge, power, and will.
RAZI:1:7/r60.anchor: الكلام عبارة عن فعل مخصوص يفعله الحي القادر لأجل أن يعرف غيره ما في ضميره

RAZI:1:7/r61.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r61.speaker: المعتزلة
RAZI:1:7/r61.claim: The Muʿtazila say imperative forms signify the speaker's will, while declarative forms indicate the speaker's belief that the stated matter is so.
RAZI:1:7/r61.anchor: قالت المعتزلة : صيغة «افعل » لفظة موضوعة لإرادة الفعل

RAZI:1:7/r62.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r62.speaker: أصحابنا
RAZI:1:7/r62.claim: Razi's school distinguishes inward request from will and mental judgment from belief; God's command that an unbeliever believe is not evidence that He wills that belief.
RAZI:1:7/r62.anchor: الطلب النفساني مغاير للإرادة ، والحكم الذهني أمر مغاير للاعتقاد

RAZI:1:7/r63.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r63.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r63.claim: Razi argues that God commands the unbeliever to believe without willing it: causal determination and God's prior knowledge of disbelief each rule out the contrary belief occurring.
RAZI:1:7/r63.anchor: أنه تعالى أمر الكافر بالإيمان ، وهذا متفق عليه ، ولكن لم يرد منه الإيمان

RAZI:1:7/r64.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r64.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r64.claim: A speaker's mental judgment can differ from belief: someone may say the world is eternal while believing it is not, showing the two are distinct.
RAZI:1:7/r64.anchor: وقد يقول القائل بلسانه هذا مع أنه يعتقد أن العالم ليس بقديم

RAZI:1:7/r65.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r65.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r65.claim: A word's referent may itself be another word: technical terms such as noun, verb, particle, general, and specific name linguistic expressions.
RAZI:1:7/r65.anchor: وقد تكون مدلولاتها أيضا ألفاظا كقولنا : اسم ، وفعل ، وحرف

RAZI:1:7/r66.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r66.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r66.claim: Language is known through transmission, either mass-transmitted or solitary, and through a mix of transmission and reasoning; the majority's combined inference from exception and its effect is weak because it assumes the language-maker accepts the inference.
RAZI:1:7/r66.anchor: وعلى هذا الطريق تعويل الأكثرين في إثبات أكثر اللغات ، وهو ضعيف

RAZI:1:7/r67.author: Fakhr al-Dīn al-Rāzī
RAZI:1:7/r67.speaker: author
RAZI:1:7/r67.claim: Although some question whether language is mass-transmitted because even Allah, faith, disbelief, and grammatical forms are disputed, Razi says the underlying transmitted usage is certainly mass-transmitted.
RAZI:1:7/r67.anchor: والحق أن ورود هذه الألفاظ في أصول هذه الموارد معلوم بالتواتر
